title: GOD CREATED THE BODY, SCRIPTURE CELEBRATES MARITAL DESIRE, AND THE GOSPEL REDEEMS OUR SEXUAL BROKENNESS—So Why Should Shame Get the Final Word?
paragraphs: GOD CREATED THE BODY, SCRIPTURE CELEBRATES MARITAL DESIRE, AND THE GOSPEL REDEEMS OUR SEXUAL BROKENNESS—So Why Should Shame Get the Final Word?

What if some of the shame you have carried for years was never the voice of holiness at all? What if Jesus did not come merely to forgive what you have done with your body—but to redeem the broken story you have believed about your body, your desires, your marriage, your failures, and yourself?
There are things Christians know how to confess out loud.
But then there are other things.
Things we bury beneath worship songs and Sunday clothes.

Things hidden behind browser histories, strained marriages, private memories, unwanted thoughts, old violations, secret habits, nights we desperately wish we could erase, and questions we are terrified to ask because somewhere along the way we became convinced that even admitting the struggle would make God recoil from us.
Things we hated ourselves for wanting.
And sometimes the shame becomes so deeply attached to our identity that we no longer say, “I sinned.”
We say something far more devastating.
“God could forgive other people…but if everyone knew what was inside me, they would never look at me the same way again.”
Maybe you have never spoken those words.
Maybe you did not need to.
Maybe you have been living them.
And this is where we need to go back.
Not to whatever happened to you when you were sixteen, twenty-six, forty-six, or last night.
Before lust twisted another person into an object.
Before bodies were bought, sold, abused, compared, filtered, exposed, violated, idolized, or hated.
Genesis gives us an astonishing sentence about the first husband and wife:
"וַיִּֽהְי֤וּ שְׁנֵיהֶם֙ עֲרוּמִּ֔ים הָֽאָדָ֖ם וְאִשְׁתּ֑וֹ וְלֹ֖א יִתְבֹּשָֽׁשׁוּ"
“The man and his wife were both naked, and they were not ashamed.” — Genesis 2:25.
Before sin entered the human story, nakedness between husband and wife was not portrayed as contamination.
The body was not God's embarrassing mistake.
Sexual difference was not an accident heaven regretted.
Marriage was not humanity's concession to animal instinct.
And before humanity ever learned how to distort sexuality, God had already declared His creation good.
Because Christianity is not fundamentally a religion teaching people to hate their bodies.
The biblical story is something far more beautiful.
And Jesus came not to teach us to call corruption good, but to redeem sinners from corruption and restore us to holiness.
Because there are two lies constantly competing for your soul.
One says, “If you desire it, it must be good.”
The other says, “If you experience sexual desire at all, you must be dirty.”
But neither is desire automatically shameful.
In fact, anyone who thinks the Bible is embarrassed by marital desire has probably forgotten that the Bible contains the Song of Songs.
Listen to this extraordinary Hebrew declaration:
“I belong to my beloved, and his desire is for me.” — Song of Songs 7:10.
Not hidden in some forbidden manuscript.
Not smuggled into the Bible by modern culture.
The Song of Songs celebrates the longing, delight, attraction, exclusivity, and embodied affection of lovers within its poetic world.
The Bible does not need pornography to teach us that desire exists.
Pornography takes something profoundly human and tears it away from covenant, dignity, faithfulness, and love. It turns persons into consumable images. Lust says, “Your body exists for my appetite.”
Covenant love says something radically different.
That is why biblical holiness is not the destruction of sexuality.
It is sexuality brought under the lordship of God.
And that lordship gives us boundaries.
Scripture does not celebrate every sexual impulse simply because it feels sincere.
Touto gar estin thelēma tou Theou, ho hagiasmos hymōn…
“This is the will of God, your sanctification…”
And Paul immediately connects that sanctification with abstaining from porneia—sexual immorality—and living in holiness and honor rather than uncontrolled lust. — 1 Thessalonians 4:3–5.
Christianity says something infinitely more demanding and infinitely more hopeful.
Your body belongs under the lordship of Jesus Christ.
Your sexuality belongs under the lordship of Jesus Christ.
Your desires belong under the lordship of Jesus Christ.
Your wounds belong under the healing authority of Jesus Christ.
Jesus does not merely want the religious compartment of your life.
And this is precisely why biblical sexual ethics should never be reduced to “God hates sex.”
“Τίμιος ὁ γάμος… καὶ ἡ κοίτη ἀμίαντος.”
Marriage is honorable, and the marriage bed is amiantos—undefiled. — Hebrews 13:4.
Notice what Scripture does in the same verse.
It honors marriage and the marriage bed while also warning that God judges sexual immorality and adultery.
The Bible refuses our culture's false choice between sexual indulgence and sexual shame.
And Paul becomes surprisingly direct when speaking to married Christians.

He tells husbands and wives to fulfill their marital responsibilities toward one another. Then he uses deliberately reciprocal language about their bodies and tells spouses not to deprive one another except temporarily by mutual agreement. — 1 Corinthians 7:3–5.
Read the passage carefully and something remarkable appears.
Not one spouse treating the other like property.
And even temporary abstinence in the passage is connected with mutual agreement.
Biblical marital intimacy must never be twisted into permission for abuse, coercion, humiliation, or domination.
Sexual violence is not marital intimacy.
Using Scripture to force another person's body into submission to selfish appetite is not a defense of biblical sexuality. It is a distortion of it.
Biblical intimacy is inseparable from the wider biblical commands to love, faithfulness, self-giving, holiness, and honor.
When describing the “one flesh” union of husband and wife, he says:
And then he says he is speaking about Christ and the church. — Ephesians 5:31–32.
Even the deepest covenant intimacy between husband and wife becomes a signpost pointing beyond itself toward something greater—the faithful covenant love between Christ and His people.
And suddenly sexuality is neither god nor garbage.
It is not worthy of worship.
It is not worthy of contempt.
It belongs beneath the throne of Jesus.
But maybe none of that feels comforting to you yet.
Because your story did not happen in Eden.
Your story happened after the fall.
Maybe your sexual history does not feel like Song of Songs.
Maybe somebody introduced you to pornography before you were old enough to understand what it would eventually do to your mind.
Maybe your spouse does not know.
Maybe your marriage carries years of rejection and resentment that nobody at church sees.
Maybe someone touched you when they had no right to.
Maybe someone who should have protected you exploited you instead.
What someone did to you was not made righteous because your body was involved.
Being sinned against does not make you the guilty party for another person's evil.
Or maybe you were the one who crossed the line.
Maybe you keep returning to images you promised God you would never look at again.
Maybe you crossed boundaries in a relationship and afterward stared at yourself wondering:
Now we have arrived at the place shame loves most.
Because shame wants to take something you did and transform it into a permanent name.
But then Paul writes one of the most breathtaking sentences in the New Testament.
After naming serious patterns of sin, including sexual immorality and adultery, he turns toward believers whose pasts were anything but spotless.
Then come three thunderclaps of grace:
“In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God.” — 1 Corinthians 6:9–11.
Paul does not pretend sin was harmless.
The Gospel does not require us to rename darkness as light.
The Gospel announces that darkness does not have to own us forever.
Jesus does not save us by pretending sin never mattered.
He saves sinners at the cost of His own blood.
The cross simultaneously destroys two lies.
“My sin is too serious for Jesus.”
This is where some Christians have accidentally confused shame with repentance.
“What I did was sin. Jesus, turn me around.”
“What I did is what I am, and there is no road home.”
Shame often tells a different story: that Christ's blood may cleanse other people, but somehow your particular stain survived Calvary.
And if Christ has washed you, who gave shame permission to keep calling you permanently filthy?
This does not mean consequences disappear.
Pornography may require radical changes in access, habits, secrecy, and community.
Some wounds may require wise pastoral care and qualified professional help.
Repentance is not pretending nothing happened.
Forgiveness is not calling evil good.
Grace is not permission to continue destroying yourself or someone else.
Jesus forgives sinners and calls them into transformed lives.
That balance appears vividly in the familiar account recorded in John 8.
Some churches have shouted “sin no more” so loudly that broken people never heard “neither do I condemn you.”
Others have emphasized “neither do I condemn you” while becoming uncomfortable with “sin no more.”
We need a Savior tender enough to receive the ashamed and holy enough to refuse to leave us enslaved.
Maybe that is what your soul has been starving for.
Not another person telling you sexual sin does not matter.
Not another person acting as though sexual struggle makes you uniquely disgusting.
And still calls sinners to come.
David knew something about sexual sin.
He knew desire could become coveting.
He knew coveting could become adultery.
He knew adultery could become deception.
He knew concealed sin could spread devastation far beyond a private moment.
And after his sin was exposed, his prayer was not:
“Create in me a clean heart, O God.” — Psalm 51:10.
Help everybody think I am clean.
Create in me a clean heart.
There is the difference between reputation management and repentance.
Some of us have spent years trying to make sure nobody discovers what Jesus has been asking us to surrender.
But eventually grace brings us to the place where excuses can no longer heal us.
And strangely, confession—the thing shame told you would destroy you—becomes the doorway toward freedom.
Because the Gospel is not the announcement that good people can become slightly better.
The Gospel is the announcement that Jesus Christ saves sinners.
People whose stories look like scandals.
People who have carried what was done to them for decades.
This is why you cannot understand Christian sexuality without understanding the cross.
At the cross, Jesus does not merely tell you to try harder.
The condemned sinner is offered justification.
The ashamed can learn to stand before God clothed not in self-righteousness but in Christ.
And the resurrection announces that your worst chapter does not possess the authority to write your ending.
Maybe your marriage has become cold.
Maybe pornography has hollowed out places inside you.
Maybe you are single and exhausted from fighting desires nobody knows about.
Maybe adultery shattered your home and you would give anything to rewind time.
Maybe someone violated you, and for years you have confused what was done to you with who you are.
Maybe you have repented but cannot forgive yourself.
Then perhaps the question is no longer whether your feelings pronounce you clean.
The question is whether Christ's verdict is greater than your feelings.
The Gospel does not say your past never happened.
It says your past does not get to be your savior, your master, or your final identity.
Your scandal is not stronger than His grace.
Your temptation is not stronger than His Spirit.
Your wound is not beyond His compassion.
Your body is not beyond His claim.
Your marriage is not beneath His concern.
Your sexuality is not a room Jesus is embarrassed to enter.
Tell Him what you keep wanting.
Tell Him what you cannot seem to stop.
Tell Him what was done to you.
Tell Him why you are angry.
Tell Him why intimacy terrifies you.
Tell Him why you feel unwanted.
Tell Him why you keep going back.
Tell Him the sentence you have never dared to say in prayer.
Seek wise help where wounds run deep.
Confess sin instead of negotiating with it.
Ask trusted, mature believers for accountability rather than fighting every battle alone.
And when the accuser drags an old file across the courtroom of your mind, remember the grammar of grace:
Jesus Christ does not merely edit scandals.
And perhaps someone reading this is shaking a little because this article touched the room inside your heart that you have kept locked for years.
You do not have to tell strangers every detail of your story.
He already knows the unedited version.
Let somebody know that behind the polished profile picture there is a real human being who still needs grace.
There may also be somebody on your Facebook friends list who will never walk into a pastor's office and say, “I'm struggling sexually.”
They may never tell their family.
But they might read something you share at 1:37 in the morning when nobody else is awake.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God.
Send it privately to the person who would never admit publicly that they need it.
If this ministry is helping you know Christ more deeply, there is another way you can help carry the message farther.
Not because salvation is for sale.
And not as a substitute for faithful generosity and responsibility in your local church.

And if God has blessed you with the ability to give, supporting Gospel work can itself be an act offered for His glory when it flows freely from faith, gratitude, love, and obedience—not fear, manipulation, or an attempt to purchase spiritual favor.
The goal is not merely more content.
More wounded believers reminded of grace.
More hidden battles brought into light.
More Christians strengthened to follow Jesus when nobody is applauding.
More marriages pointed toward covenant faithfulness.
More prodigals reminded that the Father's house is not closed.
More sinners hearing that repentance is possible because mercy is real.
Because Gospel Warrior cannot wash you.
A pastor cannot carry your sin away.
A ministry cannot resurrect your heart.
“God could never use someone with your history…”
Christianity itself is filled with redeemed histories.
Paul had blood on his résumé.
The Corinthian church had sexual brokenness serious enough for Paul to confront directly.
That is why shame does not get the final word.
Pornography does not get the final word.
Adultery does not get the final word.
Abuse does not get the final word.
Your divorce does not get the final word.
Your virginity does not save you.
Your sexual history does not automatically damn you.
Your desires are not your god.
Your wounds are not your identity.
Your failures are not your master.
Your body belongs beneath the lordship of Christ.
Your wounds can be brought into the light.
Your life can become an offering of holiness.
Your story can still become a testimony.
Because the final word over every repentant sinner who has taken refuge in Christ is not:
And maybe that is the sentence you needed tonight.
You thought Jesus was standing at the end of your story holding a red pen.
Perhaps you forgot He walked to a cross carrying scars.
The chapter you are most ashamed to let anyone read may become the very place where people someday discover how fiercely Jesus Christ knows how to redeem.
